claim: Blood cell counts often fail to report on immune processes occurring in remote tissues.
source: Blood cell counts often fail to report on immune processes occurring in remote tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a limitation of current methods.

claim: Immune cell type-specific methylation patterns in circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) can be used for studying human immune cell dynamics.
source: Here, we use immune cell type-specific methylation patterns in circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) for studying human immune cell dynamics.
evidence: This is the main methodological approach described in the abstract.

claim: Immune cfDNA levels had no individual steady state as opposed to blood cell counts.
source: Immune cfDNA levels had no individual steady state as opposed to blood cell counts, suggesting that cfDNA concentration reflects adjustment of cell survival to maintain homeostatic cell numbers.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: cfDNA concentration reflects adjustment of cell survival to maintain homeostatic cell numbers.
source: Immune cfDNA levels had no individual steady state as opposed to blood cell counts, suggesting that cfDNA concentration reflects adjustment of cell survival to maintain homeostatic cell numbers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed lack of steady state in immune cfDNA levels.

claim: Following influenza vaccination (N = 92), B-cell-derived cfDNA levels increased prior to elevated B-cell counts.
source: Following influenza vaccination (N = 92), B-cell-derived cfDNA levels increased prior to elevated B-cell counts and predicted efficacy of antibody production.
evidence: This is a key finding from the vaccination study reported in the abstract.

claim: B-cell-derived cfDNA levels predicted efficacy of antibody production following influenza vaccination.
source: Following influenza vaccination (N = 92), B-cell-derived cfDNA levels increased prior to elevated B-cell counts and predicted efficacy of antibody production.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by data in the results section.

claim: Patients with eosinophilic esophagitis (N = 21) showed selective elevation of eosinophil cfDNA.
source: Patients with eosinophilic esophagitis (N = 21) and B-cell lymphoma (N = 27) showed selective elevation of eosinophil and B-cell cfDNA, respectively, which were undetectable by cell counts in blood.
evidence: This is a key finding from the EoE study reported in the abstract.

claim: Patients with B-cell lymphoma (N = 27) showed selective elevation of B-cell cfDNA.
source: Patients with eosinophilic esophagitis (N = 21) and B-cell lymphoma (N = 27) showed selective elevation of eosinophil and B-cell cfDNA, respectively, which were undetectable by cell counts in blood.
evidence: This is a key finding from the lymphoma study reported in the abstract.

claim: Selective elevation of eosinophil and B-cell cfDNA in EoE and lymphoma patients were undetectable by cell counts in blood.
source: Patients with eosinophilic esophagitis (N = 21) and B-cell lymphoma (N = 27) showed selective elevation of eosinophil and B-cell cfDNA, respectively, which were undetectable by cell counts in blood.
evidence: This demonstrates the advantage of cfDNA analysis over blood cell counts.

claim: A major limitation of circulating immune cell analysis is that it often fails to report on immune processes taking place in remote locations.
source: A major limitation of circulating immune cell analysis is that it often fails to report on immune processes taking place in remote locations.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the introduction.

claim: CRP and similar proteins reflect the presence of tissue inflammation but are highly non-specific with regard to tissue location and the nature of inflammatory process.
source: Conversely, CRP and similar proteins do reflect the presence of tissue inflammation but are highly non-specific with regard to tissue location and the nature of inflammatory process (Gabay and Kushner, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current biomarkers, supported by citation.

claim: Dying cells release nucleosome-size fragments of cell-free DNA (cfDNA), which travel transiently in blood before being cleared by the liver.
source: Dying cells release nucleosome-size fragments of cell-free DNA (cfDNA), which travel transiently in blood before being cleared by the liver (Heitzer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cfDNA biology, supported by citation.

claim: Liquid biopsies using cfDNA have been applied to reveal the presence of mutations in a fetus as reflected in maternal cfDNA.
source: Liquid biopsies using cfDNA have been applied to reveal the presence of mutations in a fetus as reflected in maternal cfDNA (Bianchi et al., 2014; Fan et al., 2012; Lo et al., 1997), identify and monitor tumor dynamics via the presence of somatic mutations in plasma (Wan et al., 2017), and detect the rejection of transplanted organs when the levels of donor-derived DNA markers are elevated in recipient plasma (De Vlaminck et al., 2014; De Vlaminck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an established application of cfDNA analysis, supported by citations.

claim: cfDNA analysis has been used to identify and monitor tumor dynamics via the presence of somatic mutations in plasma.
source: Liquid biopsies using cfDNA have been applied to reveal the presence of mutations in a fetus as reflected in maternal cfDNA (Bianchi et al., 2014; Fan et al., 2012; Lo et al., 1997), identify and monitor tumor dynamics via the presence of somatic mutations in plasma (Wan et al., 2017), and detect the rejection of transplanted organs when the levels of donor-derived DNA markers are elevated in recipient plasma (De Vlaminck et al., 2014; De Vlaminck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an established application of cfDNA analysis, supported by citation.

claim: cfDNA analysis has been used to detect the rejection of transplanted organs when the levels of donor-derived DNA markers are elevated in recipient plasma.
source: Liquid biopsies using cfDNA have been applied to reveal the presence of mutations in a fetus as reflected in maternal cfDNA (Bianchi et al., 2014; Fan et al., 2012; Lo et al., 1997), identify and monitor tumor dynamics via the presence of somatic mutations in plasma (Wan et al., 2017), and detect the rejection of transplanted organs when the levels of donor-derived DNA markers are elevated in recipient plasma (De Vlaminck et al., 2014; De Vlaminck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an established application of cfDNA analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Tissue-specific DNA methylation patterns can be used to determine the tissue origins of cfDNA.
source: More recently, we and others have shown that tissue-specific DNA methylation patterns can be used to determine the tissue origins of cfDNA, allowing to infer cell death dynamics in health and disease even when no genetic differences exist between the host and the tissue of interest (Cheng et al., 2019; Lehmann-Werman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a key methodological foundation for the study, supported by citations.

claim: The majority of cfDNA in healthy individuals originates in hematopoietic cells.
source: Although the majority of cfDNA in healthy individuals is known to originate in hematopoietic cells (Lehmann-Werman et al., 2016; Moss et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2015), it has often been regarded as background noise, against which one may look for rare cfDNA molecules released from a solid tissue of interest.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cfDNA composition, supported by citations.

claim: Dozens of uniquely hypomethylated CpG sites were identified for most immune cell types examined.
source: We identified dozens of uniquely hypomethylated CpG sites for most cell types examined, qualifying these as biomarkers for DNA derived from a given cell type (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the marker identification analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 17 different CpG sites were selected whose combined methylation status could distinguish the DNA of seven major immune cell types: neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, B-cells, CD3 T-cells, CD8 cytotoxic T-cells, and regulatory T-cells.
source: Based on this in silico comparative analysis, we selected for further work 17 different CpG sites, whose combined methylation status could distinguish the DNA of seven major immune cell types: neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, B-cells, CD3 T-cells, CD8 cytotoxic T-cells, and regulatory T-cells (Tregs).
evidence: This describes the marker panel developed for the study.

claim: The methylation marker cocktail can quantitatively detect the presence of DNA from specific immune cell types even when blood DNA was diluted 10- to 20-fold.
source: The markers quantitatively detected the presence of DNA from specific immune cell types even when blood DNA was diluted 10- to 20-fold (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from spike-in experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A strong correlation was observed between assessments of specific cell fractions using CBC and DNA methylation patterns (Pearson's correlations; r = 0.67–0.83, p-value < 0.0001).
source: Comparing the CBC to DNA methylation pattern, we observed a strong correlation between assessments of specific cell fractions in the two methods (Pearson's correlations; r = 0.67–0.83, p-value < 0.0001, Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), supporting validity of the methylation assay for identifying fractions of DNA derived from specific immune cell types, consistent with previous findings (Baron et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a validation finding comparing methylation markers to CBC, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The proportion of cfDNA from specific immune cell types did not correlate well with the proportion of the same markers in circulating blood cells and with CBC (Pearson's correlations; r = 0.14–0.53).
source: However, comparing cfDNA methylation markers in plasma to blood DNA methylation markers and CBC, we observed that proportion of cfDNA from specific immune cell types did not correlate with the proportion of the same markers in circulating blood cells and with CBC (Pearson's correlations; r = 0.14–0.53, Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a key finding showing cfDNA differs from blood cell proportions, shown in Figures 2B-C.

claim: Immune cfDNA levels are the result of biological processes beyond immune cell counts.
source: These findings suggest that immune cfDNA levels are the result of biological processes beyond immune cell counts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of correlation between cfDNA and cell counts.

claim: The fraction of lymphocyte cfDNA in plasma was always smaller than the fraction of lymphocyte DNA in circulating blood cells or the fraction of lymphocytes in CBC.
source: For example, the fraction of lymphocyte cfDNA in plasma was always smaller than the fraction of lymphocyte DNA in circulating blood cells or the fraction of lymphocytes in CBC (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), in agreement with the long half-life of lymphocytes compared with other blood cell types (Macallan et al., 2005; Michie et al., 1992).
evidence: This finding is consistent with the long lifespan of lymphocytes, supported by citations.

claim: The fraction of monocyte cfDNA was larger than the fraction of monocyte DNA in genomic DNA from whole blood or the fraction of monocytes in CBC.
source: Conversely, the fraction of monocyte cfDNA was larger than the fraction of monocyte DNA in genomic DNA from whole blood or the fraction of monocytes in CBC (Figure 2B–C), consistent with the shorter half-life of monocytes (Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: This finding is consistent with the short lifespan of monocytes, supported by citation.

claim: Deconvolution of WGBS data revealed that lymphocyte cfDNA was under-represented relative to the abundance of DNA from these cells in blood (p-value = 0.002).
source: This analysis, based on genome-wide methylation patterns, also revealed that lymphocyte and monocyte cfDNA was under- and over-represented, respectively, relative to the abundance of DNA from these cells in blood (lymphocytes, p-value = 0.002; monocytes, p-value = 0.0005, Kruskal-Wallis) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from WGBS deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Deconvolution of WGBS data revealed that monocyte cfDNA was over-represented relative to the abundance of DNA from these cells in blood (p-value = 0.0005).
source: This analysis, based on genome-wide methylation patterns, also revealed that lymphocyte and monocyte cfDNA was under- and over-represented, respectively, relative to the abundance of DNA from these cells in blood (lymphocytes, p-value = 0.002; monocytes, p-value = 0.0005, Kruskal-Wallis) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from WGBS deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neutrophils were the main source of immune-derived cfDNA in healthy individuals (mean = 390, range 10–1064 genome equivalents [GE]/ml).
source: Consistent with our previous plasma methylome analysis (Moss et al., 2018), we found that neutrophils were the main source of immune-derived cfDNA (mean = 390, range 10–1064 genome equivalents [GE]/ml), followed by monocytes (mean = 101, range 6–233 GE/ml), eosinophils (mean = 38, range 0–111 GE/ml) and lymphocytes (T-cells, mean = 30, range 1-79; B-cells, mean = 17, range 3–42; CD8 T-cells, mean = 8, range 0–27; Tregs, mean = 2, range 0–9 GE/ml) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of 227 healthy donors, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In circulating blood cells, the inter-individual variation in immune methylation markers and CBC was always higher than the intra-individual variation.
source: In circulating blood cells, the inter-individual variation in immune methylation markers and CBC was always higher than the intra-individual variation in these markers (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Blood cell counts among individuals are more similar to themselves than to others, indicating distinct set points per person for the total number of specific immune cell types circulating in blood.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that blood cell counts among individuals are more similar to themselves than to others, indicating distinct set points per person for the total number of specific immune cell types circulating in blood (Alpert et al., 2019; Carr et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about blood cell count stability, supported by citations.

claim: cfDNA values of immune methylation markers varied to the same extent among samples of the same individual and among samples of different individuals.
source: Strikingly, cfDNA values of the same immune methylation markers varied to the same extent among samples of the same individual and among samples of different individuals (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a key finding from longitudinal analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: B-cell counts were moderately but significantly elevated on day 7 post-vaccination, and persisted to day 28 (p-value = 0.0048).
source: Consistent with previous reports, B-cell counts (measured by methylation analysis of DNA from whole blood) were moderately but significantly elevated on day 7, and persisted to day 28 (p-value = 0.0048, Kruskal-Wallis) (Figure 3A; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the vaccination study shown in Figure 3A, consistent with previous reports.

claim: B-cell-derived cfDNA levels increased as early as day 3 post-vaccination, peaked on day 7 and returned to baseline levels on day 28 (p-value < 0.0001).
source: Surprisingly, B-cell-derived cfDNA levels increased as early as day 3, peaked on day 7 and returned to baseline levels on day 28 (p-value < 0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis) (Figure 3B and D), suggesting that cfDNA reveals an early increase in the turnover of B-cells following vaccination, which is not portrayed in circulating B-cells.
evidence: This is a key finding from the vaccination study shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: Total cfDNA levels did not change over the time course of vaccination.
source: Of note, this response was specific to B-cell-derived cfDNA; total cfDNA levels did not change over the time course of vaccination, nor did cfDNA levels of other immune cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This demonstrates the specificity of the B-cell cfDNA response, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: cfDNA levels of other immune cell types did not change over the time course of vaccination.
source: Of note, this response was specific to B-cell-derived cfDNA; total cfDNA levels did not change over the time course of vaccination, nor did cfDNA levels of other immune cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This demonstrates the specificity of the B-cell cfDNA response, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Responders to vaccination had a significantly higher peak elevation of B-cell cfDNA relative to their pre-vaccination baseline levels compared with non-responders (p-value = 0.044).
source: Responders had a significantly higher peak elevation of B-cell cfDNA relative to their pre-vaccination baseline levels compared with non-responders (p-value = 0.044, Mann-Whitney, AUC = 0.7, p-value = 0.04) (Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a key finding linking B-cell cfDNA to vaccination efficacy, shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Peripheral B-cell counts were not different between responders and non-responders to vaccination (p-value = 0.2).
source: Peripheral B-cell counts were not different between responders and non-responders (p-value = 0.2, Mann-Whitney) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This demonstrates that B-cell counts do not predict vaccination response, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Influenza vaccination is more effective in younger individuals.
source: It is well established that influenza vaccination is more effective in younger individuals (Del Giudice et al., 2015; Ranjeva et al., 2019; Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009; Wagner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about vaccination efficacy, supported by citations.

claim: Non-responders to vaccination were all above 35 years and tended to have a minimal elevation of B-cell cfDNA above baseline.
source: Non-responders to vaccination in our cohort were all above 35 years and tended to have a minimal elevation of B-cell cfDNA above baseline even when compared to people in their age group (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, peak elevation of B-cell cfDNA in responders versus non-responders p-value = 0.089), suggesting that B-cell cfDNA dynamics report on a biological process independent of age.
evidence: This is a finding from age-stratified analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: EoE is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized clinically by esophageal dysfunction, and histologically by eosinophil-predominant inflammation of the esophagus.
source: EoE is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized clinically by esophageal dysfunction, and histologically by eosinophil-predominant inflammation of the esophagus (Liacouras et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EoE, supported by citation.

claim: Diagnosis of EoE requires an invasive endoscopic biopsy.
source: Diagnosis of EoE requires an invasive endoscopic biopsy.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current EoE diagnosis.

claim: Most EoE patients do not show peripheral eosinophilia.
source: Notably, most patients do not show peripheral eosinophilia (Aceves et al., 2007; Dellon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EoE, supported by citations.

claim: Patients with active EoE had elevated levels of eosinophil cfDNA (mean = 115 GE/ml) compared with healthy controls (mean = 34 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0056).
source: Patients with active EoE had elevated levels of eosinophil cfDNA (mean = 115 GE/ml) compared with both healthy controls (mean = 34 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0056) and patients with inactive EoE (mean = 36 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0003, Kruskal-Wallis), while other immune cfDNA markers were not elevated in active EoE patients (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a key finding from the EoE study shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Patients with active EoE had elevated levels of eosinophil cfDNA compared with patients with inactive EoE (mean = 36 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0003).
source: Patients with active EoE had elevated levels of eosinophil cfDNA (mean = 115 GE/ml) compared with both healthy controls (mean = 34 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0056) and patients with inactive EoE (mean = 36 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0003, Kruskal-Wallis), while other immune cfDNA markers were not elevated in active EoE patients (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a key finding from the EoE study shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Other immune cfDNA markers were not elevated in active EoE patients.
source: Patients with active EoE had elevated levels of eosinophil cfDNA (mean = 115 GE/ml) compared with both healthy controls (mean = 34 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0056) and patients with inactive EoE (mean = 36 GE/ml, p-value = 0.0003, Kruskal-Wallis), while other immune cfDNA markers were not elevated in active EoE patients (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This demonstrates the specificity of eosinophil cfDNA elevation in EoE, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The fraction of eosinophils in blood was not significantly elevated in EoE patients (p-value=0.1).
source: The fraction of eosinophils in blood was not significantly elevated in EoE patients (Figure 4C and p-value=0.1, Kruskal-Wallis), consistent with restriction of eosinophil abundance to the esophagus and further supporting the idea that immune cfDNA is not a reflection of circulating immune cells.
evidence: This demonstrates that eosinophil counts do not reflect EoE disease activity, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Eosinophil cfDNA could distinguish active EoE from healthy controls (AUC 0.83, p-value = 0.001).
source: Eosinophil cfDNA could distinguish active EoE from healthy controls (Figure 4E, AUC 0.83, p-value = 0.001) and from patients with inactive disease (Figure 4F, AUC 0.84, p-value = 0.0001), with high specificity and sensitivity.
evidence: This is a finding from ROC analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Eosinophil cfDNA could distinguish active EoE from patients with inactive disease (AUC 0.84, p-value = 0.0001).
source: Eosinophil cfDNA could distinguish active EoE from healthy controls (Figure 4E, AUC 0.83, p-value = 0.001) and from patients with inactive disease (Figure 4F, AUC 0.84, p-value = 0.0001), with high specificity and sensitivity.
evidence: This is a finding from ROC analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Lymphoma patients (mean = 264.4 GE/ml) had dramatically elevated levels of B-cell-derived cfDNA compared with controls (mean = 18.3 GE/ml, p-value < 0.0001).
source: Lymphoma patients (mean = 264.4 GE/ml) had dramatically elevated levels of B-cell-derived cfDNA compared with controls (mean = 18.3 GE/ml, p-value < 0.0001), while B-cell counts in peripheral blood were actually decreased (control; mean = 0.162, lymphoma; mean = 0.079, 109/l, p-value = 0.0059, Mann-Whitney) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a key finding from the lymphoma study shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: B-cell counts in peripheral blood were decreased in lymphoma patients (control; mean = 0.162, lymphoma; mean = 0.079, 109/l, p-value = 0.0059).
source: Lymphoma patients (mean = 264.4 GE/ml) had dramatically elevated levels of B-cell-derived cfDNA compared with controls (mean = 18.3 GE/ml, p-value < 0.0001), while B-cell counts in peripheral blood were actually decreased (control; mean = 0.162, lymphoma; mean = 0.079, 109/l, p-value = 0.0059, Mann-Whitney) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This demonstrates that B-cell counts do not reflect lymphoma disease burden, shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The level of B-cell cfDNA accurately distinguished B-cell lymphoma patients from healthy controls (AUC = 0.98, p-value < 0.0001).
source: We observed that the level of B-cell cfDNA accurately distinguished B-cell lymphoma patients from healthy controls, much better than did B-cell counts (cfDNA, AUC = 0.98, p-value < 0.0001; B-cell counts, AUC = 0.75, p-value = 0.006; Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from ROC analysis shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: B-cell counts distinguished B-cell lymphoma patients from healthy controls less accurately than B-cell cfDNA (AUC = 0.75, p-value = 0.006).
source: We observed that the level of B-cell cfDNA accurately distinguished B-cell lymphoma patients from healthy controls, much better than did B-cell counts (cfDNA, AUC = 0.98, p-value < 0.0001; B-cell counts, AUC = 0.75, p-value = 0.006; Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from ROC analysis shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Total levels of cfDNA were elevated in lymphoma patients.
source: Total levels of cfDNA as well as the levels of other immune cfDNA markers were also elevated in lymphoma patients, consistent with reports on alterations in non-B-cells in lymphoma (Simone, 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the lymphoma study, consistent with previous reports.

claim: The strongest cfDNA response in lymphoma was observed in B-cells (14.4-fold increase), CD8 cytotoxic T-cells (10.7-fold), and Tregs (13.8-fold).
source: We observed the strongest response in the levels of B-cell cfDNA (14.4-fold increase compared with controls), CD8 cytotoxic T-cells (10.7-fold), and Tregs (13.8-fold) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the lymphoma study shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A decrease in B-cell-derived cfDNA was observed in most lymphoma patients after treatment (n = 16, p-value = 0.0032).
source: In an additional cohort of lymphoma patients that were monitored before and after treatment, we observed a decrease in B-cell-derived cfDNA in most patients (n = 16, p-value = 0.0032, Kruskal-Wallis test), similarly to what have been observed in other cancers following treatment (Moss et al., 2020; Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal monitoring of lymphoma patients, shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The vast majority of unique methylation loci are hypomethylated in the cell type of interest and methylated elsewhere.
source: Notably, across the entire atlas, the vast majority of such unique loci are hypomethylated in the cell type of interest and methylated elsewhere (typically marking cell type-specific enhancers), while just a small minority are methylated in a given cell type and hypomethylated elsewhere (manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is a finding from the methylation atlas analysis.

claim: Unique methylation loci typically mark cell type-specific enhancers.
source: Notably, across the entire atlas, the vast majority of such unique loci are hypomethylated in the cell type of interest and methylated elsewhere (typically marking cell type-specific enhancers), while just a small minority are methylated in a given cell type and hypomethylated elsewhere (manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genomic location of methylation markers.

claim: The concentration of cfDNA from a given cell type is a function of the total number of cells of that type, the lifespan of this population, determinants of cfDNA release, and determinants of cfDNA clearance from plasma.
source: Specifically, the concentration of cfDNA derived from a given immune cell type is a function of the total number of cells of that type (circulating and remote pools, combined), the lifespan of this population, determinants of cfDNA release (e.g. efficiency of phagocytosis) and determinants of cfDNA clearance from plasma (e.g. liver uptake).
evidence: This is a theoretical model explaining cfDNA dynamics.

claim: Methylation markers can inform on the turnover dynamics of cell types, not cell states.
source: We note however that dynamic cellular states may involve changes in gene expression that do not involve reprogramming of DNA methylation patterns, representing a limitation of the approach. In other words, methylation markers can inform on the turnover dynamics of cell types, not cell states.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the methylation-based approach.

claim: Lower levels of neutrophil cfDNA were observed in adult females compared with adult males.
source: For example, we noticed lower levels of neutrophil cfDNA in adult females compared with adult males, suggesting that neutrophils in females live longer; we speculate that such differences in lifespan explain why women have a higher steady-state neutrophil count (Bain and England, 1975) (and data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the healthy cohort analysis.

claim: Women have a higher steady-state neutrophil count.
source: For example, we noticed lower levels of neutrophil cfDNA in adult females compared with adult males, suggesting that neutrophils in females live longer; we speculate that such differences in lifespan explain why women have a higher steady-state neutrophil count (Bain and England, 1975) (and data not shown).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Elevated monocyte cfDNA and reduced lymphocyte cfDNA were observed in individuals older than 60.
source: Additional observations of healthy immune cfDNA dynamics that merit further investigation regard age-related changes, such as elevated monocyte cfDNA and reduced lymphocyte cfDNA in individuals older than 60.
evidence: This is an observation from the healthy cohort analysis.

claim: Varying cfDNA levels reflect the action of regulated cell death as a homeostatic mechanism by which the healthy body maintains cell numbers within a desired range.
source: We propose that varying cfDNA levels reflect the action of regulated cell death as a homeostatic mechanism by which the healthy body maintains cell numbers within a desired range (model, Figure 6).
evidence: This is a proposed model to explain cfDNA dynamics, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Elevated B-cell turnover reflects early stages in the successful response of B-cells to the vaccine, including the process of affinity maturation.
source: We propose that elevated B-cell turnover (and elevated B-cell cfDNA as its readout) reflects early stages in the successful response of B-cells to the vaccine, including the process of affinity maturation whereby large numbers of B-cells are generated and eliminated within lymph nodes as a result of insufficient binding to the target epitope.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the B-cell cfDNA elevation after vaccination.

claim: In lymphoma, immune cfDNA processes include both tumor dynamics and host responses.
source: As with EoE, cfDNA in lymphoma provides a systemic biomarker of immune processes taking place in remote locations. However in lymphoma, these processes include both tumor dynamics and host responses – either bystander effects (collateral damage) or an immune response to the tumor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multiple immune cfDNA elevations observed in lymphoma.

claim: An important current limitation of immune repertoire analysis is that it requires large genomic fragments, which can only be derived from whole cells.
source: An important current limitation of immune repertoire analysis is that it requires large genomic fragments, which can only be derived from whole cells. This precludes cfDNA-based analysis, and limits access to T- and B-cell dynamics taking place in remote locations.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of immune repertoire analysis.

claim: Immune repertoire analysis is precluded from cfDNA-based analysis and limits access to T- and B-cell dynamics taking place in remote locations.
source: An important current limitation of immune repertoire analysis is that it requires large genomic fragments, which can only be derived from whole cells. This precludes cfDNA-based analysis, and limits access to T- and B-cell dynamics taking place in remote locations.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of immune repertoire analysis.

claim: Both T/B repertoire analysis and expression profiling can be complemented by cfDNA profiling, which will provide non-overlapping information about immune cell turnover in remote locations.
source: We propose that both T/B repertoire analysis and expression profiling can be complemented by cfDNA profiling, which will provide non-overlapping information about immune cell turnover (and potentially also gene expression patterns associated with cell death) (Sadeh et al., 2021) in remote locations.
evidence: This is a proposed application of cfDNA analysis to complement other methods.
